name: Cavity mode counting and the Planck law
summary: The density of electromagnetic standing-wave modes in a cavity, 8πν²/c³, times the mean energy per mode gives the blackbody spectrum: equipartition (k_BT per mode) yields Rayleigh–Jeans and the ultraviolet catastrophe, while Bose–Einstein occupation of each mode as a quantum oscillator yields Planck's law.
breaks: Weyl mode counting needs cavity size ≫ λ; in sub-wavelength cavities and photonic crystals the density of states is engineered and the free-space Planck law no longer applies.
sources: Planck (1901). "Ueber das Gesetz der Energieverteilung im Normalspectrum". *Ann. Phys.* 309, 553. [doi:10.1002/andp.19013090310](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19013090310)

name: Radiation pressure and the Stefan–Boltzmann law
summary: The Maxwell stress tensor gives isotropic radiation the pressure p = u/3; inserting this into the thermodynamic identity (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂p/∂T)_V − p forces u ∝ T⁴ (Boltzmann 1884), and the adiabatic invariant VT³ = const gives Wien's displacement law.
map: p=\frac u3,\quad \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T=T\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V-p\ \Rightarrow\ u=aT^4,\quad VT^3=\text{const (adiabatic)}

name: Planck's resonators: dipole emission balances absorption
summary: Planck obtained the factor 8πν²/c³ classically by balancing the Larmor emission of damped Hertzian dipole oscillators against their absorption of isotropic radiation; quantizing the oscillator energy then gave the Planck spectrum, so antenna theory sits at the birth of quantum statistics.
sources: Planck (1901). "Ueber das Gesetz der Energieverteilung im Normalspectrum". *Ann. Phys.* 309, 553. [doi:10.1002/andp.19013090310](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19013090310)

name: Einstein A and B coefficients from detailed balance
summary: Requiring two-level atoms in equilibrium with Planck radiation to obey detailed balance with Boltzmann populations fixes g₁B₁₂ = g₂B₂₁ and A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³; stimulated emission, the source of laser gain, is forced by the Bose–Einstein statistics of photons.

name: Johnson–Nyquist noise from a 1D blackbody line
summary: Nyquist derived thermal voltage noise by letting two resistors exchange energy through a lossless transmission line whose modes each hold k_BT, a one-dimensional blackbody; this is the first fluctuation–dissipation theorem, generalized by Callen–Welton. The same physics sets antenna noise temperature, which is how the CMB was first read.
sources: Nyquist (1928). "Thermal Agitation of Electric Charge in Conductors". *Phys. Rev.* 32, 110. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.32.110](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.32.110)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)
Penzias & Wilson (1965). "A Measurement of Excess Antenna Temperature at 4080 Mc/s". *Astrophys. J.* 142, 419. [doi:10.1086/148307](https://doi.org/10.1086/148307)

name: Dielectric function as a causal response function
summary: ε(ω) and the Drude/Lorentz models are the archetypal linear-response functions: causality makes χ analytic in the upper half-plane, giving the Kramers–Kronig relations between refraction and absorption; Im ε measures dissipation, and Kubo's formula gives the optical conductivity from equilibrium current correlations.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I.". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

name: Fluctuational electrodynamics and near-field heat transfer
summary: Rytov's fluctuational electrodynamics treats thermal emission as Maxwell fields radiated by random currents whose spectrum is fixed by the FDT (∝ Im ε). Between bodies closer than the thermal wavelength, evanescent surface plasmon and phonon polaritons carry heat orders of magnitude beyond the Stefan–Boltzmann limit; the same correlators give Casimir–Lifshitz forces.
sources: Polder & Van Hove (1971). "Theory of Radiative Heat Transfer between Closely Spaced Bodies". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3303. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3303](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3303)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Wiener–Khinchin: spectra from correlation functions
summary: The optical power spectrum is the Fourier transform of the field autocorrelation (Wiener–Khinchin), the same relation that defines noise spectral densities in linear-response theory; the FDT then ties the spectrum of thermal light to the absorptive response of the emitter.
map: S(\omega)=\int\langle E^*(t)E(t+\tau)\rangle e^{i\omega\tau}d\tau\ \leftrightarrow\ S_x(\omega)=\int\langle x(t)x(0)\rangle e^{i\omega t}dt
sources: Mandel & Wolf (1995). "Optical Coherence and Quantum Optics". Cambridge University Press. [doi:10.1017/cbo9781139644105](https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139644105)

name: Thermal light: Bose–Einstein fluctuations and bunching
summary: A single mode of thermal light has a geometric Bose–Einstein photon-number distribution with variance n̄ + n̄². The n̄² wave term is classical interference of random phasors (Gaussian statistics, g⁽²⁾(0) = 2, Hanbury Brown–Twiss bunching); the n̄ term is particle shot noise. Together they are Einstein's 1909 fluctuation formula for blackbody radiation.
map: P(n)=\frac{\bar n^n}{(1+\bar n)^{n+1}},\qquad \langle\Delta n^2\rangle=\bar n+\bar n^2,\qquad g^{(2)}(\tau)=1+|g^{(1)}(\tau)|^2
sources: Glauber (1963). "The Quantum Theory of Optical Coherence". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 2529. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.2529)
Mandel & Wolf (1995). "Optical Coherence and Quantum Optics". Cambridge University Press. [doi:10.1017/cbo9781139644105](https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781139644105)

name: Speckle as a random walk of phasors
summary: A speckle field is a sum of many phasors with random phases, a two-dimensional random walk, so by the central limit theorem it is a circular Gaussian field with exponential intensity statistics and unit contrast. Pearson posed the random-walk problem in 1905 and Rayleigh answered it from his theory of superposed vibrations of random phase.
map: A=\sum_{k=1}^Na_ke^{i\phi_k}\ \Rightarrow\ p(I)=\frac{1}{\langle I\rangle}e^{-I/\langle I\rangle},\qquad C=\frac{\sigma_I}{\langle I\rangle}=1
sources: Goodman (1976). "Some fundamental properties of speckle". *J. Opt. Soc. Am.* 66, 1145. [doi:10.1364/JOSA.66.001145](https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSA.66.001145)
Pearson (1905). "The Problem of the Random Walk". *Nature* 72, 294. [doi:10.1038/072294b0](https://doi.org/10.1038/072294b0)

name: Dynamic light scattering measures Brownian motion
summary: Light scattered by diffusing particles decorrelates as g⁽¹⁾(q,τ) = exp(−Dq²τ); with the Siegert relation and Stokes–Einstein D = k_BT/6πηa, photon-correlation spectroscopy turns Einstein's Brownian-motion theory into a routine size and dynamics probe, extended to multiple scattering by diffusing-wave spectroscopy.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Über die von der molekularkinetischen Theorie der Wärme geforderte Bewegung von in ruhenden Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 549. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053220806](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053220806)
Pusey & van Megen (1986). "Phase behaviour of concentrated suspensions of nearly hard colloidal spheres". *Nature* 320, 340. [doi:10.1038/320340a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/320340a0)

name: Critical opalescence and Ornstein–Zernike scattering
summary: Rayleigh scattering from a fluid measures its density fluctuations, I ∝ S(q) with S(0) = nk_BTκ_T (Einstein–Smoluchowski). Near a critical point κ_T and ξ diverge and the fluid turns milky; the Ornstein–Zernike angular dependence of the scattered light was a primary measurement of γ, ν and η.
sources: Einstein (1910). "Theorie der Opaleszenz von homogenen Flüssigkeiten und Flüssigkeitsgemischen in der Nähe des kritischen Zustandes". *Ann. Phys.* 338, 1275. [doi:10.1002/andp.19103381612](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19103381612)

name: Rayleigh–Brillouin spectrum and the dynamic structure factor
summary: Light inelastically scattered by a fluid shows a central Rayleigh line (heat diffusion) and two Brillouin lines (sound); their widths and the Landau–Placzek intensity ratio come from the hydrodynamic dynamic structure factor S(q,ω), which by the FDT is the absorptive part of the density response.

name: Radiative transfer as a Boltzmann equation for photons
summary: The radiative-transfer equation is a linear Boltzmann equation for the photon distribution, with extinction as the loss term and the scattering phase function as the collision kernel; its diffusion limit gives the Rosseland opacity of stellar interiors and diffuse optics in tissue, just as Chapman–Enskog gives transport coefficients.

sources: Rybicki & Lightman (1979). "Radiative processes in astrophysics". Wiley. [doi:10.1002/9783527618170](https://doi.org/10.1002/9783527618170)

name: Compton thermalization and the Kompaneets equation
summary: Repeated Compton scattering off a thermal electron gas drives photons toward a Bose–Einstein distribution with a chemical potential, since scattering conserves photon number. The Kompaneets Fokker–Planck equation, including the induced-scattering n² term, governs CMB μ- and y-distortions and the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect.
map: \frac{\partial n}{\partial y}=\frac{1}{x^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left[x^4\left(\frac{\partial n}{\partial x}+n+n^2\right)\right],\quad x=\frac{h\nu}{k_BT_e}
sources: Rybicki & Lightman (1979). "Radiative processes in astrophysics". Wiley. [doi:10.1002/9783527618170](https://doi.org/10.1002/9783527618170)
Mather et al. (1994). "Measurement of the cosmic microwave background spectrum by the COBE FIRAS instrument". *Astrophys. J.* 420, 439. [doi:10.1086/173574](https://doi.org/10.1086/173574)

name: Optical traps as the laboratory for fluctuation theorems
summary: The gradient force on a Rayleigh-regime dielectric particle, F = ½ Re(α)∇|E|², makes a tunable harmonic or double-well potential for a Brownian colloid; optical traps gave the first tests of fluctuation theorems and the measurement of Landauer's k_BT ln 2 erasure bound.
map: \mathbf F_{\rm grad}=\tfrac12\mathrm{Re}(\alpha)\nabla\langle|\mathbf E|^2\rangle,\qquad \kappa\langle x^2\rangle=k_BT,\qquad \langle W_{\rm erase}\rangle\ge k_BT\ln2
sources: Ashkin (1970). "Acceleration and Trapping of Particles by Radiation Pressure". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 24, 156. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.24.156)
Bérut et al. (2012). "Experimental verification of Landauer's principle linking information and thermodynamics". *Nature* 483, 187. [doi:10.1038/nature10872](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10872)

name: Laser threshold as a second-order phase transition
summary: Near threshold the single-mode laser field obeys a Langevin equation with a Landau-type potential whose quadratic coefficient changes sign with pump: the field amplitude is an order parameter with mean-field exponent β = 1/2, spontaneous emission is the noise, and the free phase behaves like a Goldstone mode.
map: \dot E=(a-b|E|^2)E+\xi(t)\ \Rightarrow\ V(E)=-\frac a2|E|^2+\frac b4|E|^4,\qquad a\propto P_{\rm pump}-P_{\rm th}
breaks: The laser is a driven-dissipative steady state with no free energy or detailed balance; finite photon number rounds the transition, and the effective temperature is set by spontaneous emission rather than a heat bath.
sources: DeGiorgio & Scully (1970). "Analogy between the Laser Threshold Region and a Second-Order Phase Transition". *Phys. Rev. A* 2, 1170. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.2.1170](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.2.1170)

name: Random and multimode lasers as photonic spin glasses
summary: Mode amplitudes of multimode lasers evolve under an effective Hamiltonian of four-mode couplings; with random couplings (random lasers) this is a spherical p-spin glass at an effective temperature set by noise over pump squared, and replica-symmetry breaking has been reported in shot-to-shot spectral fluctuations. Passive mode-locking is the ordered phase of the same theory.
breaks: Effective equilibrium holds only in a slow-amplitude mean-field limit; real lasers are open and dissipative, and the measured RSB overlaps are indirect.
sources: Ghofraniha et al. (2015). "Experimental evidence of replica symmetry breaking in random lasers". *Nature Commun.* 6, 6058. [doi:10.1038/ncomms7058](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms7058)
Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)

name: The three-level maser as a Carnot engine
summary: A three-level maser pumped by a hot reservoir and relaxed by a cold one is a heat engine: each emitted photon converts heat to work with efficiency ν_s/ν_p, which population inversion forces to stay below the Carnot efficiency (Scovil and Schulz-DuBois 1959), the founding example of quantum heat engines.
sources: Scovil & Schulz-DuBois (1959). "Three-Level Masers as Heat Engines". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 2, 262. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.2.262](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.2.262)

name: Optical refrigeration and the entropy of light
summary: Anti-Stokes fluorescence cooling of solids removes heat by emitting broadband, isotropic fluorescence that carries more entropy than the narrow, collimated pump; Landau's entropy of radiation keeps the second law intact and bounds the cooling efficiency.

sources: Epstein et al. (1995). "Observation of laser-induced fluorescent cooling of a solid". *Nature* 377, 500. [doi:10.1038/377500a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/377500a0)

name: Schawlow–Townes linewidth as phase diffusion
summary: Spontaneous emission kicks the laser phase randomly; above threshold the amplitude is pinned but the phase performs Brownian motion, so the field correlation decays exponentially and the line is a Lorentzian of Schawlow–Townes width, the Langevin/Fokker–Planck laser theory of Lax and Haken.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

name: Thermal-noise floor of ultrastable reference cavities
summary: Brownian motion of mirror coatings and substrates, computed with the FDT from mechanical loss angles (Levin's direct approach), sets the fundamental stability limit of Fabry–Pérot-stabilized lasers used in optical clocks and gravitational-wave detectors.
sources: Numata, Kemery & Camp (2004). "Thermal-Noise Limit in the Frequency Stabilization of Lasers with Rigid Cavities". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 93, 250602. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.250602](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.93.250602)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

name: Chemical potential of light: photon BEC versus lasing
summary: When photons thermalize by repeated absorption and re-emission in a dye-filled microcavity, their number is conserved and they acquire a chemical potential; above a critical number they Bose-condense into the lowest cavity mode, distinct from lasing, which needs inversion. Luminescent radiation from LEDs and solar cells likewise carries μ = qV (Würfel's generalized Planck law).
sources: Klaers et al. (2010). "Bose–Einstein condensation of photons in an optical microcavity". *Nature* 468, 545. [arXiv:1007.4088](https://arxiv.org/abs/1007.4088)

name: Optical NLS, inverse scattering and the Bethe ansatz
summary: Pulse propagation in a Kerr fibre obeys the integrable nonlinear Schrödinger equation, solved exactly by inverse scattering; its quantized form is the attractive delta-interacting Bose gas (Lieb–Liniger/McGuire), which Lai and Haus solved by Bethe ansatz to describe quantum optical solitons.
sources: Lai & Haus (1989). "Quantum theory of solitons in optical fibers. II. Exact solution". *Phys. Rev. A* 40, 854. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.40.854](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.40.854)

Lieb & Liniger (1963). "Exact Analysis of an Interacting Bose Gas. I. The General Solution and the Ground State". *Phys. Rev.* 130, 1605. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605)

name: Optical thermodynamics of multimode nonlinear fibres
summary: In highly multimode nonlinear waveguides the conserved optical power and Hamiltonian play the roles of particle number and energy; weak Kerr mixing drives modal occupations to a Rayleigh–Jeans distribution with an optical temperature and chemical potential, and beam self-cleaning appears as condensation into the fundamental mode.
sources: Wu, Hassan & Christodoulides (2019). "Thermodynamic theory of highly multimoded nonlinear optical systems". *Nature Photon.* 13, 776. [doi:10.1038/s41566-019-0501-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41566-019-0501-7)

name: Coherent Ising machines from degenerate OPOs
summary: A degenerate optical parametric oscillator above threshold settles into one of two phases (0 or π), an optical Ising spin; networks of time-multiplexed OPO pulses with measurement-feedback coupling search for low-energy states of Ising and Sherrington–Kirkpatrick Hamiltonians, using the pitchfork bifurcation as an annealing schedule.
sources: McMahon et al. (2016). "A fully programmable 100-spin coherent Ising machine with all-to-all connections". *Science* 354, 614. [doi:10.1126/science.aah5178](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aah5178)
Sherrington & Kirkpatrick (1975). "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 35, 1792. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792)

name: Anderson localization of light
summary: Anderson localization is a wave-interference effect, so it applies to light: John proposed strong photon localization near the band edges of disordered photonic crystals, and transverse localization has been imaged in disordered photonic lattices. Photons have no interactions or Fermi sea, so optics isolates the single-particle physics.
breaks: Absorption mimics localization in transmission measurements, and in 3D dielectrics near-field dipole coupling may prevent true Anderson localization of light.
sources: Anderson (1958). "Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices". *Phys. Rev.* 109, 1492. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.109.1492)

John (1987). "Strong localization of photons in certain disordered dielectric superlattices". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 58, 2486. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2486](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.58.2486)

name: Coherent backscattering is weak localization
summary: In a disordered medium each multiple-scattering path interferes constructively with its time-reversed partner in the exact backward direction, doubling the reflected intensity in a cone of width ~λ/ℓ*; this is the optical twin of the weak-localization correction to electrical conductance and a precursor of Anderson localization.
sources: Wolf & Maret (1985). "Weak Localization and Coherent Backscattering of Photons in Disordered Media". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2696. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696)

van Albada & Lagendijk (1985). "Observation of Weak Localization of Light in a Random Medium". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2692. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692)

name: Effective-medium theory and percolating composites
summary: The effective permittivity or conductivity of a metal–dielectric composite (Maxwell Garnett, Bruggeman) is a mean-field theory of a random network; Bruggeman's symmetric theory predicts a conductor–insulator threshold (p_c = 1/3 in 3D), and near the true percolation threshold metal films show power-law conductivity and giant local-field fluctuations.

name: Landau–Devonshire theory of ferroelectrics
summary: Spontaneous polarization in a ferroelectric is a Landau order parameter: expanding the free energy in P gives Curie–Weiss divergence of ε above T_c, hysteresis as metastable branches, and first- versus second-order transitions from the sign of the quartic term; ferromagnetic M and χ follow the same theory.

name: Langevin–Debye orientational polarizability
summary: Permanent dipoles in a field have canonical weights e^{pE cosθ/k_BT}; averaging gives the Langevin function and, at weak field, the Debye orientational polarizability p²/3k_BT, the electric twin of Curie's law for paramagnets and the microscopic origin of temperature-dependent ε and χ.

name: Magnetocaloric effect and adiabatic demagnetization
summary: Adding the field work term μ₀H·dM (or E·dP) to the fundamental relation makes H and M a conjugate pair like −p and V; the resulting Maxwell relation gives the magnetocaloric and electrocaloric effects and adiabatic demagnetization, the classic route to millikelvin temperatures.
map: dG=-S\,dT-\mu_0M\,dH,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial H}\right)_T=\mu_0\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\right)_H,\qquad \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial H}\right)_S=-\frac{\mu_0T}{C_H}\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\right)_H

name: Bohr–van Leeuwen theorem: no classical magnetism
summary: With minimal coupling H(p − qA), the classical canonical partition function is independent of A after shifting the momentum integration, so classical statistical mechanics predicts zero equilibrium magnetization; diamagnetism and paramagnetism are quantum effects. Gauge invariance of the partition function is the formal content.
map: Z=\int d^3r\,d^3p\,e^{-\beta H(\mathbf r,\mathbf p-q\mathbf A)}\ \stackrel{\mathbf p\to\mathbf p+q\mathbf A}{=}\ Z|_{\mathbf A=0}\ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf M=-\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mathbf B}=0
sources: Müller et al. (2024). "Gauge Invariance of Equilibrium Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 133, 217101. [arXiv:2406.19235](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19235)

name: Poisson–Boltzmann and Debye–Hückel as mean-field electrostatics
summary: Closing Poisson's equation with Boltzmann-distributed ion densities gives the Poisson–Boltzmann equation, a mean-field theory of electrolytes and charged colloids; linearized it yields Debye–Hückel screening, and it fails (ion correlations, like-charge attraction) exactly where fluctuations beyond mean field matter.

name: Étendue conservation and the brightness theorem
summary: Étendue n²A dΩ is the phase-space volume of a ray bundle and is conserved by any passive optical system (Liouville), so radiance cannot be increased and no lens or mirror can heat a target above the Sun's surface temperature; this is the second law in ray optics and fixes the maximum solar concentration n²/sin²θ_s.

name: Thermal emission engineering: radiative cooling and TPV
summary: Kirchhoff's law (emissivity equals absorptivity, from detailed balance) lets nanophotonic structures engineer thermal emission: daytime radiative cooling dumps heat into cold space through the 8–13 µm atmospheric window, and selective emitters push thermophotovoltaic conversion toward the Carnot and detailed-balance limits.
map: P_{\rm cool}=P_{\rm rad}(T)-P_{\rm atm}(T_{\rm amb})-P_{\rm sun}-P_{\rm cond},\qquad \epsilon(\lambda,\theta)=\alpha(\lambda,\theta)
sources: Raman et al. (2014). "Passive radiative cooling below ambient air temperature under direct sunlight". *Nature* 515, 540. [doi:10.1038/nature13883](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13883)
Shockley & Queisser (1961). "Detailed Balance Limit of Efficiency of p-n Junction Solar Cells". *J. Appl. Phys.* 32, 510. [doi:10.1063/1.1736034](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1736034)

name: Maximum-entropy image reconstruction
summary: Reconstructing an image from incomplete Fourier data (interferometer visibilities, blurred noisy images) is underdetermined; choosing the image of maximum entropy consistent with the data within the noise is Jaynes's MaxEnt inference transplanted to imaging, a standard deconvolution method in radio astronomy.
sources: Gull & Daniell (1978). "Image reconstruction from incomplete and noisy data". *Nature* 272, 686. [doi:10.1038/272686a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/272686a0)
Jaynes (1957). "Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics". *Phys. Rev.* 106, 620. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.106.620](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.106.620)

name: Shannon capacity limits of optical fibre
summary: Shannon's channel capacity bounds data rates in fibre networks; because Kerr nonlinearity makes noise grow with launch power, achievable spectral efficiency peaks at an optimum power (the nonlinear Shannon limit), tying information entropy to fibre physics.
sources: Shannon (1948). "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". *Bell Syst. Tech. J.* 27, 379. [doi:10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1948.tb01338.x)
